Principle: Custom 3D-printed phone attachment (4 blue LEDs 450–495 nm + emission filter + 25 mm achromatic lens) images Nile-Red-stained, filtered particles. · MATLAB algorithm extracts red fluorescence channel to count & size.
Detects: PS, PP, PET fluoresce well; does NOT detect black rubber/tire particles. · No chemical polymer ID — fluorescence-based only. · Reliable ≥10 µm (FOV ~490 mm², pixel ~4.7 µm).
Equipment & sample prep: Smartphone (Nokia Lumia 1020-class, 48 MP) + custom LED/lens attachment + battery · 24 mm glass-fibre filter (1.2 µm), Nile Red 0.5 µg/mL in chloroform, vacuum filtration · KI density separation + centrifuge for soil/solid matrices · Sample prep: filter → stain → 24 h air-dry (or faster vacuum-dry) → image
Cost: Prototype ≈ US$500 · "orders of magnitude" less than bench fluorescence microscopes
Accuracy / detection limit: Linear response to 135 particles/L (p<0.001) · Above that: aggregation → underestimation · Reliable down to 10 µm
Portability: Inherently portable — battery-powered LEDs, no mains power · Framed for resource-limited field use
Key limitations: Misses black/rubber particles · Needs >10 µm · High debris load needs dilution · No chemical polymer confirmation

Principle: $10 "TinyScope" clip-on microscope on an ordinary phone camera images density-separated, filtered MP. · ImageJ thresholds to binary; YOLOv5 CNN (COCO transfer-learned) detects/counts by texture/edge, not colour.
Detects: Presence/count + coarse morphology (fibre vs fragment, SEM cross-check) · No automated polymer ID or precise sizing by the DL model itself · Polymer ID confirmed separately via ATR-FTIR/SEM in the study, not by the field method
Equipment & sample prep: $10 TinyScope clip-on + smartphone · ImageJ, Label Studio, PyTorch/Colab+GPU (training only) · ZnCl₂ (1.7 g/cm³) density separation, H₂O₂ digestion, Whatman filter, vortex + ultrasonic bath · Confirmatory-only (not routine): ATR-FTIR, FE-SEM
Throughput: Extraction <1 h · Real-time/live video detection demonstrated
Accuracy / detection limit: 98% overall detection accuracy · Recall ~0.90, precision ~0.85, mAP@50 0.935 · (2490 images / 9113 annotations)
Portability: Imaging step is field-cheap · But full workflow still needs vortex mixer, ultrasonic bath, GPU for training
Key limitations: No true-negative baseline (can't compute specificity) · 431 false positives (dark pixels misread as MP) · Single-class model — no polymer/size/shape output

Principle: 3D-printed enclosure: USB digital microscope + 395 nm UV flashlight + yellow long-pass filter (blocks <550 nm) + Raspberry Pi 4 running onboard YOLOv8 + 3.5" touchscreen + power bank.
Detects: 6 polymers: ABS, Nylon, PE, PET, PS, PVC · 50–1000 µm fragments/powders · Count + bounding-box polymer ID · LOD >100 µm (microscope-resolution limited)
Equipment & sample prep: USB digital microscope, 395 nm UV flashlight (2400 mAh), yellow long-pass filter, Raspberry Pi 4, 3.5" TFT touchscreen, Eloop EW35 power bank (10,000 mAh), PLA 3D-printed case · Nile Red (>98% HPLC), acetone, Whatman No.1 filter (11 µm), vacuum filtration · Prep: 5 g sample/20 mL water, filter, air-dry 15 min, 0.025 mg/mL Nile Red in acetone (10 drops), dark-incubate 15 min
Cost: Itemised BOM: fixed hardware $139.60 total (microscope $11.26, UV flashlight $5.41, filter $11.44, RPi4 $62.35, touchscreen $14.85, power bank $20.29) · Variable cost ≈ $0.10/test · cf. FTIR ≈$0.44/sample + $30,000–50,000 capital
Accuracy / detection limit: mAP@50 0.941(train)/0.948(test) · Precision 0.878/0.888, Recall 0.879/0.882, F1 0.878/0.885 · Best: PE/Nylon 0.965; worst: PET 0.930
Portability: 22×23×20 cm box · Power bank, 3–4 h runtime · Field-deployable
Key limitations: >100 µm only · Untested on weathered/pigmented real plastics · Needs 10–40°C + low light (NR photobleaching) · Only 6 polymers validated · Manual staining → operator variability

Principle: Optical light-scattering (nephelometric) turbidity sensor + Arduino/ESP8266 + Wi-Fi. · ADC-converted voltage mapped to NTU/turbidity category; a paired ML layer (ABGBT) classifies contamination risk.
Detects: NOT microplastic-specific — general particulate/clarity proxy (silt, algae, organics also raise turbidity) · 0–100 NTU range, 4 categories · The paper's own "MP detection" labels are turbidity-threshold-derived, not lab-confirmed
Equipment & sample prep: Arduino Uno / ESP8266/ESP32, analog turbidity sensor, Wi-Fi module, 16×2 LCD, external power · No filtration/staining — direct in-situ reading
Cost: Device ≈ ₹2,500 · (cited comparators: multi-camera system ₹7,000; microscope-based system ₹20,000)
Throughput: Continuous real-time monitoring · (no numeric response-time given)
Accuracy / detection limit: Raw sensor: no NTU-level accuracy stated · Classification layer (ABGBT): 91.47% accuracy, 5.40% error, 90% noise tolerance
Key limitations: Explicitly NOT material-specific, per the authors · No validated NTU↔MP-concentration calibration curve exists yet (future work only) · Authors frame it as a pre-screening tool only, not a replacement for FTIR/Raman/microscopy

Principle: Water flows continuously through a transparent 2–4 mm sample tube. · Pulsed UV light focused via 2 collimating lenses into the tube; a photodetector on the opposite side captures particle fluorescence through a filter blocking the source UV wavelength. · Onboard unit counts particles via fluorescence-lifetime filtering + peak detection for aggregates.
Detects: Continuous-flow real-time particle counting via fluorescence · Excerpt available doesn't specify a dye/staining step
Equipment & sample prep: Sample tube, UV source + 2 collimating lenses, photodetector + 2 focusing lenses + blocking filter, signal-processing unit
Cost: Not stated — patent document, no BOM pricing
Throughput: Real-time (continuous flow), no numeric figure given
Accuracy / detection limit: Not stated in the patent excerpt
Portability: Compact flow-cell architecture, plausibly miniaturisable · No product-scale detail given (patent only, not a built/tested device)
Key limitations: Patent document only — no independent performance data · Dye/staining step, if any, not specified

Principle: 4-stage benchtop pipeline: ceramic pre-filter concentrates MPs → H₂O₂ oxidises interfering organics → electrostatic precipitator (charged plates) isolates neutral MP from remaining organics → backwash recovers concentrated sample. · Then: optical particle counter (light-scattering) for real-time size/count, and a TOC analyzer oxidises MPs, measuring released CO₂ as a mass-concentration index.
Detects: Particle count + size distribution (optical) · + total mass concentration (via TOC/CO₂ proxy)
Equipment & sample prep: Ceramic filter, H₂O₂ dosing, electrostatic precipitator, optical particle counter, TOC analyzer, backwash plumbing
Portability: 4-stage pretreatment chain reads as benchtop/instrument-grade complexity · Not a pocket-portable design as claimed in the patent
Key limitations: Patent document only — no independent performance data · High mechanical/process complexity for a portable consumer device

Principle: MP particles colliding with, adsorbing onto, or passing between electrodes perturb impedance, capacitance or current. · Several distinct lab implementations exist: graphene EIS electrodes, EPS-functionalised gold electrodes, microbial-biofilm electrochemical systems, single-particle ultramicroelectrode collision counting.
Detects: Polymer- and study-specific — reported cases include PS, PE, PMMA, nylon, PVC · No single implementation yet covers all common polymers · (one source table's size units read as µm/mm ambiguously — likely an OCR artifact in the original PDF; verify before quoting precisely)
Equipment & sample prep: Varies: graphene / gold / carbon-fibre / Pt ultramicroelectrode, reference & counter electrodes, potentiostat / impedance analyzer · Reviewers' framing: "requires no complex sample isolation or purification beforehand"
Cost: Not quantified in the review · Framed qualitatively as low-cost vs FTIR/Raman/ICP-MS
Throughput: Not quantified generally · "quick response times" per the review
Accuracy / detection limit: Reported detection limits across different studies: 0.09 mg/mL; 50 ppb (pure/tap water), 400 ppb (saline); ~10³–10⁴ particles/mL; 0.01 mg/L; 0.03 mM; down to 10⁻¹¹ M
Portability: Review frames as inherently portable/field-capable · But this is an emerging research area, not yet a mature off-the-shelf product
Key limitations: Mostly single-polymer, lab-electrode proof-of-concept studies · No standardised protocol yet · Review itself flags this as "a notable gap in research"

Principle: Fourier-pair relationship between spectrum and interferogram. · IR light through a Michelson interferometer is absorbed by molecular bonds at specific frequencies → functional-group fingerprint.
Detects: Functional groups (polymer type via spectral-library match), not individual molecules · Limited by particle size and substrate contamination · Review cites theoretical spatial resolution ~20 µm
Equipment & sample prep: Bench FTIR spectrometer, often with ATR or microscope attachment
Cost: ₹3,000–4,000/sample (IIT Guwahati, Dept. of Chemical Engineering fee schedule) · Capital cost cited in the review: benchtop from ~US$25,000; particle-finder systems US$100,000–250,000
Accuracy / detection limit: "Safe, non-destructive, highly specific to certain polymer types" (review's own framing)
Key limitations: Only functional groups, not full molecular ID · Size-limited · Substrate contamination risk

Principle: Laser-induced scattering generates a fingerprint spectrum. · Qualitative ID by comparing chemical structure to reference spectra.
Detects: High depth resolution; accurate ID even at very small particle sizes · Review cites theoretical spatial resolution ~1 mm — coarser than the FTIR figure in the same source; worth independent verification before quoting, since Raman is more commonly reported as sub-micron-capable elsewhere
Cost: ₹200–5,000/sample (MNIT Jaipur, Materials Research Centre facility charges) · Capital cost cited in the review: from ~US$50,000
Throughput: "Longer analysis times" per the review, no number given
Accuracy / detection limit: High depth resolution per the review's framing
Key limitations: Affected by dyes/additives/fluorescence → signal interference · Longer analysis times, difficult identification

Principle: High-temperature argon plasma atomises/ionises the sample. · Mass spectrometry on specific m/z values (e.g. ¹³C⁺) detects and quantifies individual particles.
Detects: Ultra-low concentrations; particle count, size distribution, elemental composition · Source ID via isotope analysis · Example cited: single-particle ICP-MS detection limit 8.4×10⁵ particles/L
Throughput: "Faster results than microscopy" per the review, no number given
Accuracy / detection limit: Ultra-low detection concentrations per the review's framing
Key limitations: Carbon-based MP detection hindered by other carbon sources (organics, microbes) · Interfering elements need calibration, often confirmed by FTIR/Raman anyway

Principle: SEM images particle morphology. · EDX (energy-dispersive X-ray) determines elemental composition.
Detects: Morphology + elemental composition (aids polymer ID) · Contaminant adsorption / toxicity assessment
Equipment & sample prep: SEM with EDX detector, sputter coater
Accuracy / detection limit: Detailed morphology imaging; elemental ID aids polymer identification
Key limitations: Time-consuming sampling · Elemental detection limits affect trace/tiny MP analysis · Similar elemental compositions can hinder differentiation

Principle: Thermal degradation into volatile compounds, separated by chromatography, identified by mass-to-charge ratio.
Detects: Polymer type ID; works across salt/soil/sediment/water with minimal interference from colour/size/shape/additives · Small sample needed
Accuracy / detection limit: Requires only a small sample; minimal matrix interference for polymer typing
Key limitations: Identifying ALL polymer types is challenging (matrix/thermal-degradation effects) · Needs internal standards · Destructive — tiny (~1.5 µL-scale) single-use capsule

Principle: Manual sorting/counting/characterisation of size-fractionated particles (1–20, 20–212, 212–500, >500 µm sieves) under a bench microscope, by trained analysts, per SOP.
Detects: Cannot confirm polymer identity alone — needs follow-up FTIR/Raman/Py-GC-MS · Most reliable >50 µm; poor for <20 µm
Cost: Not quantified — only "relatively inexpensive" vs spectroscopic/imaging tech, per the paper
Throughput: Not quantified (survey collected timing data but no number reported in text)
Accuracy / detection limit: 22-lab / 6-country blind study: raw mean recovery 45.7%; QA-corrected recovery >50 µm = 51.3%±21.7% · Sphere recovery best (95.9%); fibre recovery wildly over-reported (462.4%) · Colour misID: orange→"gold" 79.4% of the time; white→"clear" 71.1% · False positives: mean 16/median 11 of 80 spiked look-alikes called MP, per sample · Analyst experience did NOT significantly improve recovery (only precision)
Key limitations: Strong subjectivity, high inter-lab variability · Poor for <20 µm · Cannot confirm polymer ID alone

Method: Nile Red staining + RGB decision-tree ID [14]
Principle: Nile Red (hydrophobic, solvatochromic dye) binds plastic surfaces and fluoresces, emission shifting with polymer polarity. · Particles photographed under UV/blue/green filters; RGB pixel stats along max Feret diameter feed two decision-tree models (plastic-detection, polymer-ID).
Detects: 7 polymers validated (nylon, PE, PET, PP, PS, PUR, PVC) vs 10 natural materials · 50–1200 µm range · PP is the weak spot — confused with PE, sometimes missed entirely · UV filter alone can't separate plastic from fluorescing natural material (chitin/fibre co-staining, only partially solved)
Equipment & sample prep: Fluorescence microscope + camera + UV/blue/green filters (e.g. Leica DM1000), PTFE filters (10 µm), Nile Red 10 µg/mL in acetone, ImageJ + R (CART decision trees) · Independent polymer confirmation via µ-FTIR
Cost: Equipment <US$10,000 (microscope+camera+filters) · Consumables <US$5/filter · cf. benchtop FTIR from US$25k, FTIR particle-finder US$100–250k, Raman from US$50k
Throughput: ~2.5 min image + ~5 min classify per series · 20-particle sample ≈55 min vs 170 min for µ-FTIR (3–6× faster) · Whole-filter stereomicroscope imaging: ~13 min/20-MP sample
Accuracy / detection limit: Plastic-Detection Model: 95.8% CCI (κ=0.92) validation; 92.8% on spiked samples · Polymer-ID Model: 88.1% CCI (κ=0.86) validation; 80% on spiked samples · cf. µ-FTIR ~96±7%
Portability: Lab-based (microscope, filtration manifold, computer) · Authors frame LOW COST — not portability — as the accessibility win
Key limitations: PP misclassification · NR co-stains chitin/natural fibres (unresolved false-positive risk) · Untested on naturally-weathered/biofouled field MPs

Principle: UV-photographed (365 nm) filter membranes processed by an open-source Python tool (MUPL): per-channel segmentation, median-filter background removal, Canny edge detection, skeletonisation for length/thickness/shape classification.
Detects: No polymer ID (colour/fluorescence only) · Validated for FIBRES 0.4–10 mm (400–10,000 µm) — below 0.4 mm, resolution unreliable · Outputs count + morphological sizing, not just presence/absence
Equipment & sample prep: Leitz ORTHOLUX II microscope + DeltaPix camera (validation only); Sony ILCE-7RM3 SLR + Zeiss 100 mm macro + tripod rig (main photography) · Alonefire SV10 365 nm 5W UV flashlight (mains-wired) · Glass-fibre filters, optional Nile Red, 30% H₂O₂ digestion · MUPL software (Python/OpenCV/scikit-image, MIT licence, free)
Cost: Not stated — software is free/open-source; hardware costs not itemised
Accuracy / detection limit: Artificial samples: ≤13.3% deviation vs manual ImageJ count (avg <8%) · Real samples: <15–29.4% deviation (avg 10.9% unstained, improves to 8.0–8.3% with Nile Red)
Portability: Explicitly lab-only — needs a controlled dark room, mains-powered UV lamp, stabilised camera rig · Authors frame in-situ field use only as a future aspiration
Key limitations: No polymer ID · Misses <0.4 mm particles · Fluorescent mineral fractions can inflate counts · Sensitive to camera settings/timing/lighting
